 Best monitor for MacBook Pro: FAQs 
 (Image credit: Acer // Future) What is the best resolution for monitors with a MacBook Pro?
 The MacBook Pro is Apple's machine for creators, and that means having excellent visuals for photo and video editing, 3D creative work, and more. To make the most out of what you work on, 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution is the way to go. That said, if you're using your MacBook Pro for anything else, like spreadsheets, writing documents or even coding, you'll be just fine with even a 1080p display. If you're after the highest pixel density, though, 5K and upwards is what you're after. 
 What Power Delivery should the monitor have to charge my MacBook Pro?
 You'll see many monitors with Thunderbolt/USB-C Power Delivery (PD). This means you can plug your MacBook Pro into the monitor and it will charge the laptop while in use. 
 However, the right choice depends on your MacBook Pro's model and CPU. Check out the table below to see which one is right for your laptop.

 Are there any specific connectivity options that I should look for in a monitor for my MacBook Pro?
 The best monitors for a MacBook Pro will feature USB-C and/or Thunderbolt connectivity. These allow slick, single-cable connectivity that covers charging the MacBook, driving the display, and connecting peripherals. 
 Outside of that, you can find a monitor with a built-in USB-C hub that opens up several ports through the single USB-C used to send video to your monitor. Depending on the monitor, sometimes this can also be used to charge your MacBook Pro.
 Are there any monitors that are specifically designed for use with the MacBook Pro?
 Some monitors, such as the Apple Studio Display and Apple Pro Display XDR, are explicitly designed for use with Apple devices and mirror the wide color P3 gamut and Liquid Retina Display. 
 However, many high-quality monitors from other brands are also compatible with the MacBook Pro. Some monitors will work better with the MacBook Pro than others, but generally, any even semi-recent monitor will be compatible in one way or another with a MacBook Pro.
 How to choose the best monitor for MacBook Pro 
 When choosing which monitor is best for your MacBook Pro, there are a few specs and details you'll want to check.
 Not everyone will need the same specifications. For example, if you're mostly working with office apps, you may not need the broader color space coverage that's required for image or video editing. However you use your monitor, here's what we recommend looking out for.
 Resolution : macOS loves high-resolution displays. The more pixels, the better for rendering nice, clean fonts and providing plenty of image detail. Apple's own desktop displays, the Apple Pro Display XDR and Studio Display, have what's known as Retina pixel density. In practice, that means over 200 pixels per inch (PPI), which matches the screens in the MacBook Pro. Very few non-Apple displays can match that pixel density, but a 27-inch 4K display with 163 pixels per inch is a good baseline.
 Connectivity : USB-C or Thunderbolt with Power Delivery is the bare minimum when it comes to connectivity. We'd recommend at least 65W of power delivery and ideally 90W-plus for keeping your MacBook Pro fully powered. A USB hub with plenty of USB-A and USB-C ports is very desirable, too. Additional inputs like HDMI can be handy, and an Ethernet port can be useful for some office environments. The ability to daisy chain a second monitor is also an interesting option, as is a KVM switch if you're sharing the display with a second computer.
 HDR versus SDR support: HDR is a tricky technology. Many workflows don't require it. But it is becoming more widespread. A display with HDR capability tends to also offer increased colour coverage and generally improve image quality. However, the technologies that enable HDR rendering vary hugely, and some displays are much more effective than others. For that reason, unless you know your workflows require full HDR support, we recommend focusing on getting a display with good SDR performance. If it happens to also offer some HDR capability, great. But for most users, HDR probably isn't a top priority.
 Build quality and extras: It's easy to obsess over specifications like resolution and HDR performance. But the overall quality of a display and feature set can make a big difference, too. If you're paying big bucks, it's nice to have a display that feels worth the money and looks good with your laptop. Likewise, superficially lesser features like good speakers, a great webcam and a microphone array can make a big difference to the overall usability of a monitor. Having features like that built in can also help to reduce desk clutter and simplify docking and connectivity. For more extras, we've reviewed the best MacBook Pro accessories .
 How we test the best monitors for MacBook Pro 
 (Image credit: Future) Our expert team of reviewers has tested a massive range of displays, including the best monitors for photo editing and the best monitors for video editing . So, we're experienced at knowing what to look out for to help you find the best dual monitor set-up to go with your laptop.
 A decent monitor for your MacBook Pro isn't going to be cheap. So, you want to know you're making the right choice. That's why we test each display extensively. That starts with performance assessments of various aspects of image quality.
 That includes brightness, refresh rate, and pixel response. We also consider colour accuracy, viewing angles, contrast, HDR performance, latency, and last but by no means least, resolution and pixel density. Display tech is increasingly varied and complex, what with new technologies like HDR, mini-LED backlights, and OLED panels revolutionising the industry. So, we keep on top of all of that for you, helping you to understand the difference between a few edge-lit dimming zones and a real full-array deal
 Crucially, we also assess how well a display works with macOS. Once connected to a MacBook Pro, does it offer a full range of optimised scaling options, for instance? Next up is connectivity. We consider the range of ports on offer and whether single-cable docking with power delivery is included, along with USB hubs and other features like Ethernet, a KVM switch, and display daisy chaining.
 We also consider any extra features like webcams and speakers. In theory, they can add significant value. But if they're not done well, you're probably just paying for things you'll hardly ever use. You might even end up paying twice if you find you need to buy a dedicated webcam or speakers.
 Next up, there's build quality, design, and ergonomics. A monitor that looks great on the desk with your MacBook Pro is important. But good build quality matters, too. When you are investing a lot of money, you want a display to not just look good, but feel good and last the test of time.
 Then there's ergonomics. At a minimum, a robust and stable stand with a good range of adjustability, including height and tilt, is important. The ability to rotate into portrait mode can be handy, too.
 Of course, how all of those factors fit into the overall value proposition is the final measure. The MacBook Pro is a demanding machine. So, you're not going to get the best out of it with a budget display. But you can also spend a lot of money and not necessarily get a better display solution. Best Docking Station for MacBook Air M4 & M5 ~ Plugable Technologies
 Skip to content
 TL;DR
 With the lid open, the M4 and M5 MacBook Air will drive two external monitors via the TBT4-UDZ while keeping the internal display active.
 Closing the lid does not unlock support for a third external monitor. The native hardware limit for the base M4 and M5 chips is two external displays.
 A standard USB-C hub uses only a fraction of the laptop's available bandwidth. A Thunderbolt 4 dock utilizes the full 40Gbps bandwidth.
 The TBT4-UDZ is fully compatible with both the M4 and M5 — no firmware updates or software drivers are required.
 To connect three or more external monitors, you need a DisplayLink-driven dock like the UD-ULTC4K.
 Introduction
 The MacBook Air M4 and M5 are exceptional laptops, boasting pro-level performance and an upgraded display architecture that finally allows two external monitors while the laptop remains open. However, to build a true desktop workstation, the ultra-thin Air still requires a connectivity hub. For anyone who needs to run two external screens, an Ethernet connection, extra USB ports, and fast charging — all from one cable — a Thunderbolt 4 dock is the definitive answer. This guide covers exactly what MacBook Air M4 and M5 users need to complete their desk setup and why the TBT4-UDZ is the recommended docking station.
 What the MacBook Air M4 and M5 Are Missing
 While the M4 and M5 chips deliver incredible processing power, the physical chassis remains minimalist. Here is what is missing out of the box:
 Video outputs: 0 built-in (display only via Thunderbolt port)
 Max external displays: 2 (supported with the lid open or closed)
 USB-A ports: 0
 SD card slot: 0
 Ethernet: 0
 HDMI or DisplayPort: 0
 One cable connected to a premium Thunderbolt 4 dock instantly restores all of this missing functionality.
 Why Thunderbolt 4 — Not Just USB-C
 When shopping for a dock, it is critical to understand the difference between Thunderbolt and standard USB-C:
 The MacBook Air M4 and M5 feature two Thunderbolt 4 ports, which also carry USB4 and USB-C signals.
 A standard USB-C hub uses only a fraction of the laptop's available bandwidth, often bottlenecking display resolution or transfer speeds.
 A Thunderbolt 4 dock utilizes the full 40Gbps bandwidth. This enables dual 4K displays, lightning-fast data transfers, and up to 100W charging simultaneously, without any performance degradation.
 For MacBook Air users who want dual 4K monitors alongside a full suite of peripheral ports, Thunderbolt 4 is the only protocol that delivers everything at once.
 TBT4-UDZ — What It Adds to Your MacBook Air
 The Plugable TBT4-UDZ transforms your MacBook Air into a powerhouse desktop PC alternative. Rather than a list of specs, here is what it practically adds to your workflow:
 Up to Dual 4K 60Hz monitors natively: Connect two displays via a flexible mix of 2x DisplayPort 1.4 and 2x HDMI 2.0 ports.
 100W charging (98W certified): More than enough power to keep the MacBook Air fully charged while working under heavy loads.
 6x USB-A ports: Connect legacy peripherals, external drives, and accessories your Air cannot natively support.
 Front-facing 10Gbps USB-A: Fast data access without reaching around to the back of the dock.
 Rear-facing 10Gbps USB-C: Great for dedicated external storage like an SSD or external hard drive.
 Up to 2.5Gbps Ethernet: A stable, wired connection critical for reliable video calls and large file transfers.
 SD/MicroSD card readers: High-speed access for photographers and content creators.
 Total connectivity: 16 ports added to your MacBook Air from a single Thunderbolt 4 cable.
 Recommended for MacBook Air M4 and M5
 For the MacBook Air M4 and M5, the TBT4-UDZ is the cleanest, single-cable solution to unlock your dual-monitor setup, a full port suite, and reliable 100W charging.
 View the TBT4-UDZ 
 Setting Up Dual Monitors with MacBook Air M4/M5
 Setting up your extended workspace is a simple plug-and-play process:
 Connect the TBT4-UDZ to your MacBook Air using the included Thunderbolt 4 cable.
 Connect the power adapter to the dock (the dock will immediately begin charging the Air).
 Connect Monitor 1 to the dock's DisplayPort or HDMI output in “Group 1”.
 Connect Monitor 2 to the dock's second DisplayPort or HDMI output in “Group 2”.
 Open System Settings → Displays on your Mac to arrange the virtual screens to match your physical desk layout.
 Ergonomic Choice: Unlike older MacBook Air models that required closing the laptop (clamshell mode) to use two external screens, the M4 and M5 chips natively support this setup. You can leave the lid open for a three-screen setup, or close it to save desk space.
 Can I Use the TBT4-UDZ with the Lid Open?
 Yes. With the lid open, the M4 and M5 MacBook Air will drive two external monitors via the TBT4-UDZ while keeping the internal display active. This yields a highly productive three-screen total workspace.
 Note that closing the lid does not unlock support for a third external monitor. The native hardware limit for the base M4 and M5 chips is two external displays, regardless of the laptop's physical lid position.
 MacBook Air M4 vs M5 — Any Difference for Docking?
 When choosing a docking station, the experience between the two chip generations is identical:
 Both the M4 and M5 Air share the same Thunderbolt 4 port configuration.
 Both support the same external display architecture (two external displays natively, regardless of lid position).
 The TBT4-UDZ is fully compatible with both — no firmware updates or software drivers are required.
 If you are buying a dock today, the TBT4-UDZ will remain fully compatible through future upgrades with any Mac featuring Thunderbolt or USB4.
 Alternatives — When the TBT4-UDZ Isn't the Right Fit
 While the TBT4-UDZ is the premier choice, different setups have different requirements:
 Need more power: The TBT4-UDZ easily covers the MacBook Air's power draw. However, if you share the dock with a 16-inch MacBook Pro under sustained heavy load, you may want to use Apple's 140W MagSafe charger alongside the dock.
 Shopping on a strict budget: If you are under $100, a USB-C hub will add ports but won't support dual displays on a Mac. If you need dual monitors on a budget, the UD-6950Z is a more affordable alternative utilizing DisplayLink technology.
 Need 3+ external displays: The TBT4-UDZ maximizes the Mac's native limit of two external screens. To bypass Apple's limit and connect three or more external monitors, you need a DisplayLink-driven dock like the UD-ULTC4K .

 Yes. With the lid open, the M4 and M5 MacBook Air will drive two external monitors via the TBT4-UDZ while keeping the internal display active. The native hardware limit for the base M4 and M5 chips is two external displays, regardless of the laptop's physical lid position.

 A standard USB-C hub uses only a fraction of the laptop's available bandwidth, often bottlenecking display resolution or transfer speeds. For MacBook Air users who want dual 4K monitors alongside a full suite of peripheral ports, Thunderbolt 4 is the only protocol that delivers everything at once.

 No. Closing the lid does not unlock support for a third external monitor. The native hardware limit for the base M4 and M5 chips is two external displays, regardless of the laptop's physical lid position.

 When choosing a docking station, the experience between the two chip generations is identical. Both the M4 and M5 Air share the same Thunderbolt 4 port configuration, and the TBT4-UDZ is fully compatible with both — no firmware updates or software drivers are required.

 The TBT4-UDZ maximizes the Mac's native limit of two external screens. To bypass Apple's limit and connect three or more external monitors, you need a DisplayLink-driven dock like the UD-ULTC4K.

 Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.
 While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.
 The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
 The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.
 For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer .
 Add external displays to your MacBook
 If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk. Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac .
 You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI). Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac. DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.
 More explained: we cover more on Mac docking stations and external displays at the end of this feature below our recommendations.
 Do I need a docking station?
 With three TB4 or TB5 and an HDMI port, a MacBook with a Max chip could connect to up to four external displays without the need for a dock, although such a power user would likely require extra Thunderbolt and other ports for more devices to make up for using all the laptop ports for multiple monitors. See below our list of recommended docking stations for more detail on the external display options with each recent MacBook .
 All docks come with a bunch of USB ports: some old-school USB-A and newer, more capable USB-C . MacBook Pros also have an SD card reader . Although this card reader is rated as UHS-II (312MBps), Apple has pegged it back at 250MBps, so for the fastest speeds (and a microSD slot if you need one), a dock will likely be a better choice for memory-card use if it is rated at UHS-II rather than UHS-I (104MBps).
 MacBooks also lack wired Internet access via an Ethernet port, so if you want to escape flaky Wi-Fi, buy a dock with at least Gigabit Ethernet, although you could add a Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter instead if you have a spare TB port. Some later docks include faster 2.5Gb, 5Gb or even 10Gb Ethernet but you’ll need a supporting router or other device to get the benefits, although these faster Ethernet ports are backwards compatible with Gigabit so will future-proof your purchase.
 While docking stations are most often attached to MacBooks, they can be useful with a desktop Mac. The Mac mini especially can benefit from the extra ports and built-in SSD slot options. We cover these specifically in our feature on how to upgrade the Mac mini , including reviews of the best hubs and docks that fit the mini. 
 Dock or hub?
 If you need just a few extra ports, a USB-C hub or Thunderbolt hub might be your best choice—see our roundup of the best USB-C and Thunderbolt hubs for Mac . However, if you require a bunch of fast ports including Gigabit (or faster) Ethernet and multiple video ports plus more powerful charging capability, then look for a full dock that fulfils your needs. While most docks allow you to connect different computers, a KVM dock makes it easier with a special “Switch”—a button that you push to instantly take control from the other computer. The KVM Switch virtually disconnects the first computer and connects the second without you having to unplug any cables.
 The iDock M10 from AV Access is a Mac-dedicated KVM dock that you can connect to a MacBook and a desktop computer, including a Windows PC. It comes with a KVM Wired Remote Controller, which is the button you press to toggle between computers. The dock features 15 ports but four of them are used as upstream connections to the two computers.

 Which ports are on each MacBook?
 Of Apple’s recent laptop ranges, the M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air and 14-inch M3 MacBook Pro feature two ports that Apple specified as “ Thunderbolt / USB 4 ” ports, while more recent the 13in and 15in M4/M5 MacBook Air models feature two Thunderbolt 4 ports . The 14in and 16in M1/M2/M3 Pro, plain M4/M5 MacBook Pro, and M1/M2/M3 Max MacBook Pro models come with three Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) ports. Ignore Apple’s dual designation of non-4 Thunderbolt and USB4—it just means that the ports don’t certify as pure Thunderbolt 4, and that shouldn’t worry most users except for the number of external displays each supports.
 Apple’s latest M4/M5 Pro and M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro models feature three of the latest Thunderbolt 5 ports, which are backwards compatible with TB4, TB3 and USB-C. They promise 80Gbps data transfer and 120Gbps video rates. Until the technology finds its way into more devices and the Thunderbolt 5 dock market matures, you are still going to do very well with a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 dock, but Thunderbolt 5 docks are fast becoming the norm for new releases.
 Thunderbolt 5 frees the latest top-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBooks from the two-display limitation forced on them by the macOS’s lack of MST (Multi Stream Transport) support. The M5 Pro now supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt connection and the M5 Max up to four. To reach four external displays most docks reviewed here would need to daisy-chain the fourth display off one of the others.
 The entry-level MacBook Neo utilizes lower-spec USB-C rather than Thunderbolt, with 10Gbps rather than Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps or 80Gbps. A USB-C dock is therefore all you should need but it will work with Thunderbolt, which is backwards compatible, but limited to the Neo’s 10Gbps bandwidth.

 Mac docking stations and external displays
 Baseus
 While Apple’s MacBooks featuring the company’s own M-series Silicon chips are super speedy compared to the models sporting Intel processors, models with plain (non-Pro or -Max) M1 and M2 chips come with an incredible limitation: they don’t support more than one external display in Extended Mode even via their Thunderbolt ports. Plain M3 MacBooks can support two displays but only with their lids closed. The MacBook Neo uses a different A18 Pro chip and has the same single-monitor limitation as the plain M1 and M2.
 This limitation means that when using any docking station, M1/M2 and Neo MacBook users cannot extend their desktop over two or more displays, and will be limited to either dual Mirrored displays or one external display—although adding third-party DisplayLink or InstantView software to the Mac and connecting to a dedicated USB-C dock will allow you to add more than one external monitor to an M1, M2 or M3 MacBook . Follow that link for our roundup of the best USB-C DisplayLink docks , and we’ve included our favorite in our roundup above.
 In the example above, standard M1/M2/Neo Macs would require DisplayLink to achieve Extended Mode 2. M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max and standard M3/M4/M5 onwards can natively work in that mode without DisplayLink but would require it for three or more extended screens. M5 Pro supports three screens, and M5 Max supports four, without requiring DisplayLink.
 Above, we’ve listed the native external display options for each MacBook. Thunderbolt 5 docks should support up to four 6K displays if you own an M5 Max-chip MacBook Pro.
 While some docking stations promise support for 8K displays, Macs are limited to 6K support via the dock. Macs with an M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip can support an 8K display at 60Hz but only when it is connected via the Mac’s own HDMI port and not any port on the dock.
 Dock, hub or dongle: Whole lotta ports
 You need one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although the 14/16in MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe port), and likely at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
 There are many inexpensive USB-C dongles/hubs that let you add more devices to a MacBook (see our roundup of the best USB-C adapters for Macs ) or a Thunderbolt hub offering a few extra ports might be all your need, but for maximum flexibility check out a docking station that takes care of all your extra port requirements, and allows you to simply attach it to your laptop with just one cable when you get to the office or come home.
 Docks aren’t just for MacBooks. Mac mini (2018 and later) and iMac (2017 and later) owners may also consider expanding their ports with a Thunderbolt docking station.
 The inclusion of an SD or microSD card reader isn’t just for camera buffs. It’s a convenient and affordable way to add storage to your laptop setup. We found a 512GB Samsung Evo microSD card on Amazon for around $100 in the US and under £100  in the UK. That’s a very cheap way of adding half a terabyte of portable storage. For more details read up on our best microSD cards .
 Some of the docks reviewed above include an integrated SSD enclosure that lets you add up to 8TB of fast storage to your connected MacBook.
 Charging the laptop
 While the MacBook Neo can get by on 20W Power Delivery (PD), the M1/M2/M3/M4/M5 MacBook Air requires a PD charger with at least 30W power, but you can fast-charge an M2 and later Air with a charger rated at over 70W. You’ll need 67W for the 13-inch MacBook Pro and 70W for the 14-inch MBP (with 8-, 10-, 11-or 12-core CPU), 96W for 14-inch MBP (with 12- or 14-core CPU), and 96W (preferably 140W) for the 16-inch MBP. The older 15in MacBook Pro requires a 87W PD charger.
 If you own a larger MacBook Pro, buy a dock with a PD (Power Delivery) potential of at least 85W if you can. USB PD 3.0 maxes at 100W, while USB PD 3.1 can support up to 240W of power. The 16-inch MacBook Pro requires 140W to fast-charge, so owners of that laptop should look for a PD 3.1 charger.
 If you just need a spare charger, we’ve tested the best MacBook chargers for you.
 Other dock options
 Here we concentrate on Thunderbolt docks, but also include cheaper USB-C docks—which Thunderbolt MacBooks can use, but at the cost of reduced bandwidth and display limitations. We’ve also included our favorite Thunderbolt hubs for smaller and cheaper alternatives. For more non-Thunderbolt USB-C-only docks check out Tech Advisor’s roundup of the best USB-C docking stations for laptops . Tech Advisor also reviews all the available Thunderbolt 4 docks .
 Now think about a stand to go alongside the dock
 These MacBook docking stations look and work great with a laptop stand, and we’ve also tested some MacBook-friendly stands that lack all the extra ports but keep your MacBook/Air/Pro upright and out of the way: further saving valuable desk space, reducing clutter, keeping your laptop cool, and saving it from spills.

 ⚡ Quick Answer — Best Docking Station for MacBook Air
 The best docking station for MacBook Air depends on your chip and your display needs. For M3 Airs (lid closed) and M4 and M5 Airs (lid open) that support two displays, the CalDigit TS4 is the most reliable Thunderbolt 4 dock. For M1 and M2 Airs limited to one native display, a DisplayLink dock (like the Plugable UD-3900PDZ) is the only way to get dual monitors. For budget buyers, the UGREEN Revodok Max 213 offers solid TB4 performance at a lower price.
 You bought a MacBook Air for its portability. Now you want to turn it into a proper workstation. You plug in a monitor, a keyboard, an external drive, maybe a second display. Everything works — until the second monitor stays black.
 That’s the display limit trap. Apple doesn’t advertise it clearly, but your MacBook Air’s chip determines how many external displays it can drive. M1 and M2 Airs are hardware‑limited to one external display. M3 Airs support two external displays, but only when the lid is closed. M4 and M5 Airs support two with the lid open — no clamshell needed. No MacBook Air dock can bypass these limits — they’re baked into the silicon.
 This guide covers seven MacBook Air docking stations that actually work, how to choose the right MacBook Air dock based on your chip and display count, and what to do if you need dual monitors on an older Air. If you’re unsure about your chip’s limits, start with our MacBook Docking Station explainer .
 MacBook Air Dock Display Limits: Read This Before You Buy
 Before spending money on a MacBook Air docking station , check the chip. The display limit is the single most important factor.
 Chip Native External Displays Lid Requirement Workaround 
 M1 Air 1 max — hardware limit N/A DisplayLink dock for 2nd display 
 M2 Air 1 max — hardware limit N/A DisplayLink dock for 2nd display 
 M3 Air 2 max (1 with the lid open) Lid closed Thunderbolt 4 dock (check Mac support) 
 M4 Air 2 max Lid open (closing adds nothing) Thunderbolt 4 dock (check Mac support) 
 M5 Air 2 max Lid open (closing adds nothing) Thunderbolt 4 dock (check Mac support) 
 For M1 and M2 Airs, DisplayLink is the only way to get dual external monitors. Understanding this limit prevents buying a MacBook Air dock that can’t deliver what the chip can’t support.
 Apple’s current MacBook Air uses the M5 chip. For two displays on an M3 Air, Apple requires an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad, a power connection and macOS Sonoma 14.3 or later. The second display tops out at 5K at 60Hz, and it goes dark if the lid is opened with both connected. If a monitor on a dock only mirrors, Apple’s fix is to plug it into a Thunderbolt 4 port on the side of the Air instead.
 The display limit is determined by your chip — not your dock. M1 and M2 Airs max out at one external display natively. How to Choose a MacBook Air Docking Station
 Answer these three questions before reading the picks — the best docking station for MacBook Air is different for every setup. New to docks entirely? Start with Laptop Docking Stations Explained .
 1. Which chip does your MacBook Air have? 
 M1 or M2 → one native display only. If you need two monitors, buy a DisplayLink dock.
M3 → two native displays, lid closed. M4 and M5 → two native displays, lid open. A Thunderbolt 4 dock is the usual route to two displays, but check that the dock lists Mac support for your chip.
 2. How many displays do you need? 
 One display → any TB4 dock or USB‑C hub works.
Two displays → TB4 dock for M3 (clamshell) or M4 and M5 (lid open); DisplayLink dock for M1/M2.Three+ displays → DisplayLink dock only.
 3. What’s your budget? 
 Tier What You Get Example

 Premium Premium TB4, 98W+ PD, 18+ ports CalDigit TS4, Kensington SD5780T 
 🔵 Need Three Displays? The One Time a DisplayLink Dock Makes Sense
 Every Thunderbolt dock on this page is held back by your chip, not by the dock. A MacBook Air tops out at one external display (M1, M2, and the base M3 with the lid open) or two (M3 with the lid closed, M4 and M5), and no Thunderbolt dock changes that. The only way around it is a DisplayLink dock, which draws the extra screens in software through its own driver instead of the Mac’s display engine.
 If you need three screens at 4K@60Hz, the WAVLINK WL-UG69PD13 Pro is the one to look at. Two screens go through DisplayLink and the third through the dock’s HDMI Alt Mode port, which uses your Mac’s own video output.
 WAVLINK WL-UG69PD13 Pro
 WAVLINK · USB-C · DisplayLink · Gigabit Ethernet
 USB-C (DisplayLink) Triple 4K@60Hz 100W PD Driver required 15 ports 
 ✦ Best for: MacBook Air owners who need more external screens than the chip allows.
 One USB-C cable to the Mac carries the video for three screens, up to 100W of charging from the 130W adapter, wired Ethernet and the USB ports. The Mac sees two of the screens as DisplayLink displays and the third as a normal external display.
 3× HDMI and 2× DisplayPort outputs (three screens at once, one port per display group)

 Gigabit Ethernet and SD/TF card readers
 Display support: up to three 4K@60Hz screens, two through DisplayLink and one through the HDMI Alt Mode port. The Alt Mode port needs a USB-C port with video output, which the Thunderbolt ports on a MacBook Air have.
 The catch: WAVLINK states the dock does not support HDCP, so Netflix, Apple TV and other protected video won’t play while it is connected. It needs the DisplayLink Manager app plus Screen Recording permission in macOS, and a macOS update can break DisplayLink until a new driver arrives. Some Mac owners report one screen flickering. WAVLINK’s own pages also disagree on which Mac chips it covers (the Amazon listing says M1 to M5, the WAVLINK site lists M1 to M3), so check your chip and macOS version before you order.
 Verdict: If you need more screens than your Air’s chip allows, this is a dock that gets you there. If your chip already covers the screens you need, or you stream video on your external monitors, a Thunderbolt dock below is the simpler buy.

On M3 Air in clamshell, or M4 Air with the lid open, the TS4 handles dual display output reliably. On M1 and M2 Air, it drives one external display. It’s expensive, but it’s a dock you buy once and keep through multiple laptops.

 Which Is the Best Docking Station for MacBook Air? — FAQ
 Can MacBook Air run 2 monitors? 
 It depends on the chip. M1 and M2 MacBook Airs are limited to one native external display. M3 MacBook Airs support two external displays, but only when the lid is closed. M4 Airs support two with the lid open. For M1 and M2 Airs, a DisplayLink dock is the only way to get dual monitors. For a complete breakdown of chip‑specific display limits, see our  MacBook Docking Station  guide.
 Do I need Thunderbolt 4 or USB-C for MacBook Air? 
 Thunderbolt 4 is recommended for the  best docking station for MacBook Air  if you need dual 4K displays or fast data transfers. USB‑C hubs work for single‑monitor setups but can’t deliver the bandwidth required for dual displays. A MacBook Air docking station with Thunderbolt 4 guarantees 40Gbps bandwidth and native dual‑display support on M3 (clamshell) and M4 (lid open) chips. For a full comparison of the two protocols, read  USB‑C vs Thunderbolt 4 for Docking Stations .
 What is DisplayLink and do I need it? 
 DisplayLink is software‑based video compression that lets you run multiple displays over standard USB. You need it if you have an M1 or M2 MacBook Air and want dual external monitors. DisplayLink docks like the Plugable UD-3900PDZ deliver multiple displays on any Mac, but require driver installation, Screen Recording permission, and block DRM content (Netflix, Disney+, Apple TV+).
 Best budget dock for MacBook Air? 
 The UGREEN Revodok Max 213 is the  best budget docking station for MacBook Air  with Thunderbolt 4, offering dual 4K@60Hz and 90W PD at under $200. If you only need one monitor and basic USB ports, the Anker 555 is the best ultra‑budget option. For a foundational understanding of docking station architecture, see  Laptop Docking Stations Explained .
 Does a dock charge MacBook Air while I work? 
 Yes – any  best docking station for MacBook Air  with Power Delivery will charge your Air while working. The CalDigit TS4 delivers 98W, the Kensington SD5780T delivers 96W, and the Plugable TBT4‑UDZ delivers 100W. The MacBook Air draws around 30–65W under load, so even 85W is sufficient for most workflows. For a deep dive on power‑delivery failures, see  Docking Station Not Charging Laptop .

Best Docking Stations for MacBook Air M4 (2026)

 Last updated: October 29, 2026 
 Affiliate disclosure: DockYeah.com participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program. If you buy through links on this page, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. I use and test the docks and monitors I write about on my own desk, and I only recommend products I would use myself.
 Every morning, you sit down at your desk, pull out the MacBook Air M4, and plug in five cables: monitor, Ethernet, keyboard, USB drive, charger. You know this can be one cable. This guide helps you pick the dock that makes it one.
 The M4 Air changed the dock equation. For the first time on an Air, two external displays work with the lid open, with no driver and no workaround. A Thunderbolt 4 dock with two video outputs is now enough for a full dual-monitor desk. I use and test docks on my own desk with my own Macs, and I check every pick against Apple’s specs and the maker’s own documentation.
 This page is the overview for every M4 Air owner. If you want the detailed picks for your size, go to the 13-inch MacBook Air M4 dock guide or the 15-inch MacBook Air M4 dock guide . Both sizes have the same chip, ports and display limits, so the same docks work on either.
 Table of Contents
 Toggle 
 Quick Answer 
 Pick Dock Why 
 🏆 Best Overall CalDigit TS4 18 ports, 2.5GbE, SD 4.0, 98W backed by a 230W power supply 
 🖥️ Best with Built-In HDMI Plugable TBT4-UDZ Dual HDMI plus dual DisplayPort, 2.5GbE, UHS-II card readers 
 🔀 Best for Mixed Monitors Kensington SD5780T One HDMI plus Thunderbolt 4 outputs, UHS-II reader, 100W 
 🎨 Best Mac-Matching Look Plugable TBT-UDM Space gray build, driverless dual HDMI, 13 ports, 100W 
 🎒 Best for Travel (one screen) Kensington MD120U4 Compact USB4 hub, one external 4K display on a Mac, power pass-through 
 🖥️🖥️🖥️ Best for Three Monitors Plugable UD-ULTC4K Three 4K displays via DisplayLink, 100W 
 What the MacBook Air M4 Can Do With a Dock 
 Ports built into the Mac
 The M4 Air has two Thunderbolt 4 / USB4 ports, MagSafe 3 and a headphone jack. There is no HDMI, USB-A, SD card slot or Ethernet. A dock supplies everything that is missing, and plugging it into either Thunderbolt port works the same. MagSafe can stay on its own charger, which leaves both Thunderbolt ports free for data and displays.
 Display support
 The M4 Air drives two external displays natively. Apple lists up to 6K at 60Hz per display, which covers two 4K monitors with room to spare. The lid can be open or closed. That is a real change from the M3 Air, which needed the lid closed for two external displays. See Apple’s M4 Air tech specs for the exact limits.
 Charging
 Apple pairs the M4 Air with adapters up to 70W. A dock that delivers 70W or more over USB-C will charge it at the full rate. Docks at 90W to 100W are fine and leave headroom. Keep MagSafe in mind as a second way to charge if you ever want to bypass the dock.
 What to Look for in a Dock for the M4 Air 
 Thunderbolt 4 or USB-C. A Thunderbolt 4 dock gives you 40Gbps for two monitors, fast storage and Ethernet together. A good USB-C dock at 10Gbps can run two monitors and basic peripherals, but it shares one link, so it works best for lighter setups.
 Power delivery. Aim for 70W or more. Ratings are the best case: the dock also powers its own ports, so a dock with a generous power supply, like the TS4 with 230W, holds its rating under load better than one with a small adapter.
 Video outputs. For two 4K monitors at 60Hz you need HDMI 2.0 or DisplayPort. HDMI 1.4 stops at 4K 30Hz, which feels sluggish for scrolling. Check the HDMI version, not just that the port exists. If your monitors are HDMI-only and the dock has no HDMI, a short adapter fixes it.
 DisplayLink. You do not need it for two monitors on an M4 Air. It only matters for a third screen. It needs a driver, and protected streaming video does not play on DisplayLink screens.
 Port count. The Air has nothing built in, so count your permanent devices first: keyboard, mouse, webcam, drive, Ethernet, card reader.
 Best Docking Stations for the MacBook Air M4 
 1. CalDigit TS4 — Best Overall
 The TS4 is the dock I would put on a permanent M4 Air desk. It has 18 ports: three Thunderbolt 4 downstream, three USB-C and five USB-A at 10Gbps, DisplayPort 1.4, 2.5GbE, SD 4.0 and microSD 4.0 UHS-II readers, three audio jacks and a lock slot.
 The 230W power supply behind the 98W host charging is the standout. CalDigit built it so the Mac still gets full power when every port is busy. There is no built-in HDMI, so HDMI monitors need a short adapter.
 Best for: M4 Air owners who want a permanent, set-and-forget desk dock with the most ports.

 The TBT4-UDZ has two HDMI 2.0 and two DisplayPort outputs, so any pair of monitors connects without adapters. The four video ports are split into two groups, and for two screens you use one port from each group. It also has 2.5GbE, UHS-II SD and microSD readers and 100W charging. Plugable’s listing credits it as Laptop Mag’s 2025 Dock of the Year.

 The desktop replacement

 The three-monitor setup

 Known Issues and How to Fix Them 
 The second monitor does not appear

If that fails, unplug and replug the dock cable. A restart is the last resort. The only one monitor detected guide goes deeper.
 Monitors stay dark after sleep
 Disconnect and reconnect the Thunderbolt cable. If it keeps happening, update the dock’s firmware, which makers like CalDigit, Plugable and Kensington publish for their docks.
 The dock disconnects or Ethernet drops
 Check that the power adapter is seated and try the cable that came with the dock. For Ethernet, unplug and replug the cable to reset the link. If a 2.5GbE dock shows 1Gbps, your switch or router may not support 2.5GbE.

 A DisplayLink monitor shows the wrong resolution or no signal
 The DisplayLink driver has to be running. Set DisplayLink Manager to launch at login, and check that Screen Recording permission is still enabled in Privacy & Security after system updates.
 What You Should Never Buy for the M4 Air 
 Docks that mirror instead of extend
 Many inexpensive USB-C docks with two display outputs use DisplayPort MST for the second one. macOS does not support MST, so the second monitor mirrors the first. The warning sign is MST in the specs without DisplayLink or Thunderbolt. Before buying any non-Thunderbolt dock, look for explicit macOS support for extended displays, and read the questions and answers on the product page.
 Docks that cap both outputs at 4K 30Hz
 Docks with only HDMI 1.4 ports or limited USB-C video can run 4K at 30Hz, which feels choppy for scrolling and window movement. Check the HDMI version and the refresh rate in the specs.
 Thunderbolt 5 docks
 A Thunderbolt 5 dock works on the M4 Air but runs at Thunderbolt 4 speeds. You would pay for bandwidth the Mac cannot use. Save TB5 for Pro and Max machines.
 M4 Air vs M3 Air: What Changes for Dock Buyers 
 The M3 Air needed the lid closed to run two external monitors, so many owners bought a DisplayLink dock or lived in clamshell mode. The M4 Air drops that limit: two monitors, lid open, no driver. A Thunderbolt or USB-C dock with native video from your M3 days still works. What changes is that clamshell mode becomes optional, and you could replace an old DisplayLink dock with a simpler native one.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can the MacBook Air M4 run two external monitors without DisplayLink?
 Yes. The M4 Air natively supports two external displays, with the lid open or closed, without a driver. Any Thunderbolt 4 dock with two video outputs (HDMI, DisplayPort or a mix) enables it. This is a change from the M3 Air, which needed the lid closed.
 Do I need to close the lid to use two monitors?
 No. The M4 Air runs two external monitors with the lid open, so you can use the built-in screen as a third display. Clamshell mode is supported but optional.
 How much power does the M4 Air need from a dock?
 Apple’s adapters for the M4 Air go up to 70W, so a dock that delivers 70W or more charges it at the full rate. Docks at 90W to 100W are fine. MagSafe can charge in addition to the dock.
 Do I need a Thunderbolt 5 dock for the M4 Air?
 No. The M4 Air has Thunderbolt 4 ports. A Thunderbolt 5 dock runs at Thunderbolt 4 speeds on it, so the extra cost buys nothing here.
 What is the best way to run three monitors on the M4 Air?
 The M4 chip drives two external displays natively, so the third needs DisplayLink. The Plugable UD-ULTC4K is built for this. Install the driver from Synaptics and set DisplayLink Manager to launch at login. Protected streaming video does not play on DisplayLink screens.
 Can I use a USB-C hub instead of a docking station?
 For light use, yes. For a permanent desk with monitors, Ethernet and storage, a dock with its own power supply is the better choice. Many hubs share one link across everything and do not charge the Mac by themselves.
 Does the M4 Air work in clamshell mode?
 Yes. With the lid closed, the M4 Air keeps the same two-display capability and charges normally. A vertical laptop stand keeps the Mac upright and out of the way.
 Related Guides 
 Pair the dock with screens in the monitor guide for the MacBook Air M4 . If you are weighing a third screen, read DisplayLink on Mac, explained . For every Mac model, see the complete Mac docking station guide .
 Our Verdict 
 For most M4 Air owners the CalDigit TS4 is the right dock: it covers every port you could need and holds its charging under load. If your monitors are HDMI, the Plugable TBT4-UDZ spares you the adapters. If you mix HDMI and USB-C monitors, the Kensington SD5780T fits better. If you want a dock that matches the Mac, the Plugable TBT-UDM does that, and if you need a third screen the Plugable UD-ULTC4K gets you there.
 Stay away from MST-based docks that only mirror on a Mac, and from Thunderbolt 5 docks you cannot use. I set up desks like this myself, and that is the advice I would give a friend.

 Best Docking Station for MacBook Air
 The short answer
 For an M4 or M5 MacBook Air, our best-fit pick is the Plugable TBT4-UD5: it gives you two native HDMI display outputs, laptop charging, Ethernet, card readers, USB ports, and a downstream Thunderbolt port without a display driver. For an M1 or M2 Air that must run two external monitors, choose a DisplayLink model such as the Plugable USBC-6950PDZ instead —but only if you accept a driver, macOS Screen Recording permission, HDMI-only displays, and no HDCP support. For an M3 Air, the native pick can run two external displays only with the lid closed; use the DisplayLink path if two external displays must stay active while the laptop screen is open.
 Verified fact: Apple documents up to two external displays on M4 and M5 MacBook Air while the built-in display remains active. Official Apple support · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Plugable documents dual 4K 60 Hz HDMI, 13 ports, and up to 100W Power Delivery (96W certified) for the TBT4-UD5, subject to the host's display capability. Official Plugable product page · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Apple's M1 and M2 MacBook Air specifications each list one native external display up to 6K at 60 Hz. Official M1 specification · Official M2 specification · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Plugable documents two 4K 60 Hz HDMI outputs on the USBC-6950PDZ, including on computers that natively support only one display, by using DisplayLink Manager on macOS. Official Plugable product page · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Do not buy from the number of sockets alone. First identify the chip under Apple menu → About This Mac, then choose the row below. If your exact monitors, lid state, or software policy does not match a row, stop and verify before ordering.
 Buy a MacBook Air dock without guessing
 If you searched for a docking station rather than a second monitor, start with the job you need the dock to do. A dock can add ports, charging, Ethernet, and a physical connection path; it cannot raise the MacBook Air's documented native display ceiling. The practical choice is therefore host capability first, then dock video path, then the rest of the ports .
 Your actual desk goal Choose this path Stop before buying when 
 One external display, charging, wired network, and USB accessories A native Thunderbolt/USB-C dock is the low-assumption path. Match the display cable and mode to the dock's documented output. Your monitor only accepts a path the dock does not document, or its resolution/refresh exceeds the dock's stated mode. 
 Two external displays and an M4 or M5 Air Use a native dock only after matching both the Mac's two-display limit and the dock's two-output limit. The lower limit wins. Two HDMI sockets are being used as proof of support without checking the Air chip, monitor modes, and the dock's host table. 
 Two external displays and a base M3 Air Use the native path only if a closed-lid desk with power, external input devices, and the required macOS version is acceptable. The built-in screen must remain open beside both external displays; choose a documented DisplayLink route only if its software and media limits are acceptable. 
 Two external displays and an M1 or M2 Air Use a documented DisplayLink route when the second independent screen is essential; otherwise choose a native dock for one external display. Your work Mac cannot install the display software or grant Screen Recording permission, or protected video is part of the intended desk use. 
 The useful buying question is not “does this dock have two video ports?” It is “does this exact Air, with this lid state and these displays, have a documented path through this dock?” That check avoids both a needless DisplayLink purchase for a native-capable Air and a second-output purchase that cannot overcome an M1/M2 native limit.

 Why the TBT4-UD5 is the native pick
 The TBT4-UD5 is the cleanest match when the MacBook Air already supports the number of displays you need. It keeps video on the Mac's native Thunderbolt/DisplayPort path, exposes two HDMI ports for common desk monitors, and avoids a display-software dependency. The recommendation is based on the documented match below, not hands-on testing.
 Verified fact: Plugable lists two HDMI outputs up to 4K 60 Hz each, one downstream Thunderbolt 4 port up to 40 Gbps, four USB-A ports, one USB-C data port, SD and microSD readers, audio, and Gigabit Ethernet. Official Plugable product page · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Plugable says no software or display-driver installation is normally required for the TBT4-UD5. Official Plugable product page · Reviewed September 23, 2026.

 Skip this pick if your M1 or M2 Air must drive two independent external screens, your M3 must keep its built-in screen active beside two externals, or your display target exceeds the dock's documented HDMI modes. In those cases, more native-output sockets do not solve the host limit.
 Verified fact: Apple says a supported hub or Thunderbolt daisy chain can route up to two displays through one port but does not increase the maximum number of displays the Mac can support. Official Apple support · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 When the DisplayLink pick is worth it
 Choose the USBC-6950PDZ only when the workflow needs two external HDMI displays and the Air's native path cannot keep both active. It is a practical office-desk workaround, not a native display upgrade. The required DisplayLink software creates the additional display path over USB.
 Verified fact: Plugable documents two extended 4K 60 Hz HDMI displays and explicitly says DisplayLink Manager is required on macOS. Official Plugable product page · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Plugable says macOS requires Screen Recording permission for DisplayLink to send display data; without DisplayLink, only the dock's Alt Mode HDMI output works. Official Plugable support content · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Synaptics maintains the official DisplayLink Manager downloads by macOS release; check the current operating-system row before installing or updating macOS. Official Synaptics download page · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: The USBC-6950PDZ does not include its own laptop power supply: it accepts a 45W–100W USB-C charger and passes up to 82W to the host. Official Plugable power specification · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Plugable states that the USBC-6950PDZ does not support HDCP, so some protected streaming video may not play correctly on its DisplayLink outputs. Official Plugable FAQ · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Verified fact: Plugable documents HDMI displays only for this dock; a portable USB-C display cannot be connected as a display through it. Official Plugable FAQ · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Skip this pick for a managed work Mac that cannot install DisplayLink or grant Screen Recording permission, for protected-video playback on the docked screens, for USB-C-only monitors, or when you want an entirely native display path.
 Five checks before you buy
 Chip: identify M1, M2, M3, M4, or M5 in About This Mac. Do not buy from the chassis name alone.
 Screen count: write whether the laptop screen must stay on, then count the external displays separately.
 Exact modes: record every monitor's input, resolution, and refresh rate. Both recommended docks top out at 4K 60 Hz on their HDMI outputs.
 Software policy: confirm whether DisplayLink Manager and Screen Recording permission are acceptable before choosing the workaround.
 Power path: decide whether you want an included dock power supply or pass-through charging that reuses a compatible USB-C charger.
 Verified fact: On M4 and M5 Air, Apple documents up to two 6K 60 Hz or two 4K 144 Hz external displays, but the recommended TBT4-UD5's built-in HDMI outputs are documented only up to two 4K 60 Hz displays. The lower limit in the complete path wins. Official Apple display limits · Official Plugable dock limits · Reviewed September 23, 2026. 
 Connect it without guessing
 TBT4-UD5 native path
 Power the dock with its included adapter.
 Connect the supplied Thunderbolt cable from the dock's host port—the front port marked with the laptop symbol and 96W—to the MacBook Air.
 Connect one HDMI display and confirm extended mode before adding the second.
 On M3, connect power and external input devices, then close the lid before attaching or enabling the second display.
 If only one screen works, confirm the Air's chip and use the MacBook dual-monitor dock troubleshooting flow before replacing hardware.
 USBC-6950PDZ DisplayLink path
 Install the current DisplayLink Manager version from Synaptics and grant the macOS permissions it requests.
 Connect a compatible 45W–100W USB-C charger to the dock if you want pass-through charging.
 Connect the dock to the Air, then add one HDMI display at a time.
 Verify extended mode and the intended 4K 60 Hz ceiling; test protected media separately because HDCP is not supported.
 How this decision was made
 This is a documentation-based decision guide. SetupMeld did not perform hands-on testing and did not use review sites as technical sources. We compared Apple's chip-specific display limits with each manufacturer's current host, display, charging, port, driver, and known non-working conditions. The “best” label means the closest documented match for the stated scenario—not a claim that one dock is universally best.
 For an exact model-by-model comparison beyond these two picks, use the Docking Station Compatibility Matrix . If you are unsure whether the Air can run your planned screens at all, start with Can Your MacBook Run Two External Monitors? . If the labels USB4 and Thunderbolt 4 are the confusing part, use the USB4 vs Thunderbolt 4 connection-path guide .
 Sources & Verification
 Every counted fact on this page links directly to an official specification, product, or support page and carries a September 23, 2026 review date. The October 10, 2026 buying-path maintenance reorganizes those documented boundaries; it does not claim a new hands-on test or turn review material into technical evidence. Review publications, retailer listings, forums, and affiliate roundups were not used as technical evidence.

 TL;DR
 With the lid open, the M4 and M5 MacBook Air will drive two external monitors via the TBT4-UDZ while keeping the internal display active.
 Closing the lid does not unlock support for a third external monitor. The native hardware limit for the base M4 and M5 chips is two external displays.

 The TBT4-UDZ is fully compatible with both the M4 and M5 — no firmware updates or software drivers are required.
 To connect three or more external monitors, you need a DisplayLink-driven dock like the UD-ULTC4K.
 Introduction
 The MacBook Air M4 and M5 are exceptional laptops, boasting pro-level performance and an upgraded display architecture that finally allows two external monitors while the laptop remains open. However, to build a true desktop workstation, the ultra-thin Air still requires a connectivity hub. For anyone who needs to run two external screens, an Ethernet connection, extra USB ports, and fast charging — all from one cable — a Thunderbolt 4 dock is the definitive answer. This guide covers exactly what MacBook Air M4 and M5 users need to complete their desk setup and why the TBT4-UDZ is the recommended docking station.
 What the MacBook Air M4 and M5 Are Missing
 While the M4 and M5 chips deliver incredible processing power, the physical chassis remains minimalist. Here is what is missing out of the box:
 Video outputs: 0 built-in (display only via Thunderbolt port)
 Max external displays: 2 (supported with the lid open or closed)
 USB-A ports: 0
 SD card slot: 0
 Ethernet: 0
 HDMI or DisplayPort: 0
 One cable connected to a premium Thunderbolt 4 dock instantly restores all of this missing functionality.
 Why Thunderbolt 4 — Not Just USB-C
 When shopping for a dock, it is critical to understand the difference between Thunderbolt and standard USB-C:
 The MacBook Air M4 and M5 feature two Thunderbolt 4 ports, which also carry USB4 and USB-C signals.
 A standard USB-C hub uses only a fraction of the laptop's available bandwidth, often bottlenecking display resolution or transfer speeds.
 A Thunderbolt 4 dock utilizes the full 40Gbps bandwidth. This enables dual 4K displays, lightning-fast data transfers, and up to 100W charging simultaneously, without any performance degradation.
 For MacBook Air users who want dual 4K monitors alongside a full suite of peripheral ports, Thunderbolt 4 is the only protocol that delivers everything at once.
 TBT4-UDZ — What It Adds to Your MacBook Air
 The Plugable TBT4-UDZ transforms your MacBook Air into a powerhouse desktop PC alternative. Rather than a list of specs, here is what it practically adds to your workflow:
 Up to Dual 4K 60Hz monitors natively: Connect two displays via a flexible mix of 2x DisplayPort 1.4 and 2x HDMI 2.0 ports.
 100W charging (98W certified): More than enough power to keep the MacBook Air fully charged while working under heavy loads.
 6x USB-A ports: Connect legacy peripherals, external drives, and accessories your Air cannot natively support.
 Front-facing 10Gbps USB-A: Fast data access without reaching around to the back of the dock.
 Rear-facing 10Gbps USB-C: Great for dedicated external storage like an SSD or external hard drive.
 Up to 2.5Gbps Ethernet: A stable, wired connection critical for reliable video calls and large file transfers.
 SD/MicroSD card readers: High-speed access for photographers and content creators.
 Total connectivity: 16 ports added to your MacBook Air from a single Thunderbolt 4 cable.
 Recommended for MacBook Air M4 and M5
 For the MacBook Air M4 and M5, the TBT4-UDZ is the cleanest, single-cable solution to unlock your dual-monitor setup, a full port suite, and reliable 100W charging.
 View the TBT4-UDZ 
 Setting Up Dual Monitors with MacBook Air M4/M5
 Setting up your extended workspace is a simple plug-and-play process:
 Connect the TBT4-UDZ to your MacBook Air using the included Thunderbolt 4 cable.
 Connect the power adapter to the dock (the dock will immediately begin charging the Air).
 Connect Monitor 1 to the dock's DisplayPort or HDMI output in “Group 1”.
 Connect Monitor 2 to the dock's second DisplayPort or HDMI output in “Group 2”.
 Open System Settings → Displays on your Mac to arrange the virtual screens to match your physical desk layout.
 Ergonomic Choice: Unlike older MacBook Air models that required closing the laptop (clamshell mode) to use two external screens, the M4 and M5 chips natively support this setup. You can leave the lid open for a three-screen setup, or close it to save desk space.
 Can I Use the TBT4-UDZ with the Lid Open?
 Yes. With the lid open, the M4 and M5 MacBook Air will drive two external monitors via the TBT4-UDZ while keeping the internal display active. This yields a highly productive three-screen total workspace.
 Note that closing the lid does not unlock support for a third external monitor. The native hardware limit for the base M4 and M5 chips is two external displays, regardless of the laptop's physical lid position.
 MacBook Air M4 vs M5 — Any Difference for Docking?
 When choosing a docking station, the experience between the two chip generations is identical:
 Both the M4 and M5 Air share the same Thunderbolt 4 port configuration.
 Both support the same external display architecture (two external displays natively, regardless of lid position).
 The TBT4-UDZ is fully compatible with both — no firmware updates or software drivers are required.
 If you are buying a dock today, the TBT4-UDZ will remain fully compatible through future upgrades with any Mac featuring Thunderbolt or USB4.
 Alternatives — When the TBT4-UDZ Isn't the Right Fit
 While the TBT4-UDZ is the premier choice, different setups have different requirements:
 Need more power: The TBT4-UDZ easily covers the MacBook Air's power draw. However, if you share the dock with a 16-inch MacBook Pro under sustained heavy load, you may want to use Apple's 140W MagSafe charger alongside the dock.
 Shopping on a strict budget: If you are under $100, a USB-C hub will add ports but won't support dual displays on a Mac. If you need dual monitors on a budget, the UD-6950Z is a more affordable alternative utilizing DisplayLink technology.
 Need 3+ external displays: The TBT4-UDZ maximizes the Mac's native limit of two external screens. To bypass Apple's limit and connect three or more external monitors, you need a DisplayLink-driven dock like the UD-ULTC4K .

 When choosing a docking station, the experience between the two chip generations is identical. Both the M4 and M5 Air share the same Thunderbolt 4 port configuration, and the TBT4-UDZ is fully compatible with both — no firmware updates or software drivers are required.

Your MacBook Air chip must decide display compatibility before you buy.
 A MacBook Air dock can turn two USB-C ports into a one-cable desk connection for monitors, Ethernet, storage, card readers, audio, and USB accessories. The correct choice depends less on the number of ports than on whether the dock’s display technology matches the Air’s chip and whether the dock supplies the bandwidth and connections your workflow actually uses.
 Key takeaways 
 Thunderbolt 4 is the default docking-station category for MacBook Air because Apple provides two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports with charging, DisplayPort, Thunderbolt 4 up to 40Gbps, and USB4 up to 40Gbps.

 Dual-monitor compatibility depends on the exact MacBook Air chip, macOS configuration, lid position, dock, adapters, and monitor connections; no dock should be called universally dual-monitor compatible.

 This is a compatibility-first ranking rather than a port-count contest.  What should you check before buying a MacBook Air dock? 
 Check the MacBook Air chip before comparing ports or displays. Open the Apple menu and choose About This Mac , then record the chip and macOS version. Apple’s MacBook Air specification page lists the current model’s two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports with charging, DisplayPort, Thunderbolt 4 up to 40Gbps, and USB4 up to 40Gbps; the practical external-display limit still varies by generation and chip. Read Apple’s MacBook Air technical specifications alongside the dock maker’s compatibility matrix.
 Native Thunderbolt or DisplayLink?
 Native Thunderbolt is the cleanest choice for most MacBook Air owners. A Thunderbolt 4 dock uses the Mac’s native high-speed connection and native display path, normally without the extra USB graphics software required by DisplayLink. Native output is simpler for ordinary office, creative, and single-monitor setups, although the MacBook Air’s own chip limit still applies.
 DisplayLink is a specialist solution for additional screens. DisplayLink docks create display output through USB graphics, which can help base-chip MacBook Air owners exceed the number of native extended displays available from the Mac. DisplayLink requires a driver and macOS Screen Recording permission, and the USB graphics layer can introduce limitations with protected video or sleep-and-wake behavior. The Plugable UD-6950PDH product documentation is the relevant reference for this category.
 Why does the MacBook Air chip matter so much?
 MacBook Air display support is not determined by the dock alone. Plugable’s documentation distinguishes base M1 and M2 systems, base M3 systems when the lid is closed, and newer or Pro/Max systems. The Plugable TBT4-UDZ support matrix likewise shows that its dual HDMI and dual DisplayPort outputs do not behave identically across Mac chips. Treat a phrase such as dual 4K as a dock capability, not as a promise that every MacBook Air can drive two extended 4K displays.
 A clamshell requirement matters when a manufacturer documents it. If the intended setup uses the MacBook Air with its lid closed, connect power, confirm the external keyboard or mouse can wake the Mac, and check the exact chip-specific instructions before purchasing. If the lid must remain open, count only the displays supported in that configuration.
 How much charging power does a MacBook Air dock need?
 A dock’s advertised Power Delivery number is a ceiling, not a guarantee that the MacBook Air will draw that much power. A dock advertised at 90W, 98W, 100W, or 140W may reserve some power for the dock and downstream USB devices, and the MacBook Air’s charging demand is lower than that of larger MacBook Pro models. Compare host charging, the dock’s included power supply, charging while peripherals are active, and power available to connected accessories.
 Which ports matter for your workflow?
 Office and hybrid work: Prioritize HDMI or DisplayPort, USB-A for older keyboards and webcams, Ethernet, audio, and dependable host charging.
 Photography and video: Look for SD or microSD, fast USB-C, Thunderbolt, and an optional NVMe expansion slot.
 Networking: Choose 2.5GbE or 10GbE only when the Mac, dock, switch, NAS, router, cabling, and internet or local workload can use that speed.
 Travel: A bus-powered hub or a dock with an integrated power supply can reduce the number of separate items in a bag.
 Legacy peripherals: Count USB-A ports and confirm whether each port is USB 2.0, 5Gbps, or 10Gbps. A port that has the right connector can still be too slow for an external SSD.

Kensington-compatible desk installations may also benefit from a dock mounting bracket when the desk layout calls for a fixed mount.
 How do you troubleshoot a MacBook Air dock? 
 Only one monitor works
 Identify the MacBook Air chip in About This Mac.
 Check whether the dock uses native Thunderbolt output or DisplayLink.
 Read the dock’s chip-specific display matrix and confirm whether clamshell mode is required.
 Connect each monitor directly to the dock with the correct HDMI, DisplayPort, or Thunderbolt cable, then select the correct input on each monitor.
 If the dock is DisplayLink-based, install the current software and grant the required macOS Screen Recording permission.
 Test one monitor at a time before adding adapters, daisy chains, or high-bandwidth storage.
 The MacBook Air says it is not charging
 Confirm that the dock’s power supply is connected and that the host cable is attached to the dock’s charging-capable upstream port. Check whether several bus-powered USB devices are drawing power and compare the dock’s advertised host-charging figure with the power available from its included supply. A high PD rating cannot compensate for a missing or undersized dock power supply.
 Ethernet is slower than expected
 Check the negotiated link speed, the dock’s Ethernet specification, the switch or router port, the NAS or server, and the cable category. A 2.5GbE or 10GbE port reaches its target only when the connected devices and the network path support the same speed. Internet service speed can also be lower than the local wired-link speed.
 The display flickers or fails after sleep
 Reconnect the host cable, power-cycle the dock and monitor, check for firmware and macOS updates, and test without adapters or daisy-chained devices. DisplayLink setups deserve particular attention because the USB graphics software layer can affect protected video and sleep-and-wake behavior.
 Publication-time checks for a 2026 purchase 
 Confirm that the listing is the exact dock model, not a similarly named older revision.
 Verify current MacBook Air models, Apple display specifications, macOS requirements, and dock firmware notes.
 Confirm whether the dock includes its power supply and host cable.
 Match the intended monitor arrangement to the exact MacBook Air chip and determine whether clamshell mode is required.
 For DisplayLink, label the required software and Screen Recording permission before purchase.
 Check regional availability and the current Amazon listing, price, seller, stock status, and product variant immediately before publication or ordering.
 Do not treat manufacturer specifications as hands-on measurements of speed, heat, noise, or reliability.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can a MacBook Air use a Thunderbolt 5 docking station?
 Yes, a Thunderbolt 4 MacBook Air can use a Thunderbolt 5 docking station such as CalDigit TS5, but the MacBook Air remains the limiting host. The Mac will not automatically gain every Thunderbolt 5 speed or display advantage, so buy a Thunderbolt 5 dock mainly for its port design or future computers.
 Will any docking station run two monitors with a MacBook Air?
 No. A dock with two HDMI or DisplayPort outputs does not guarantee two extended displays on every MacBook Air. Native display support depends on the exact chip and configuration, while DisplayLink docks such as Plugable UD-6950PDH require software and Screen Recording permission to provide additional USB graphics displays.
 Should I choose Thunderbolt 4 or DisplayLink for a MacBook Air dock?
 Most MacBook Air owners should start with a native Thunderbolt 4 dock because native Thunderbolt avoids the additional DisplayLink software layer. DisplayLink is worthwhile when the MacBook Air’s native display limit is too low for the required number of extended screens.
 Does a higher-wattage dock charge a MacBook Air faster?
 No. A dock’s 90W, 98W, 100W, or 140W Power Delivery rating is a maximum capability, not the amount the MacBook Air must draw. The actual charging result depends on the MacBook Air, dock power supply, host port, cable, and power used by connected peripherals.
 The Bottom Line 
 Bottom line: Buy a Thunderbolt 4 dock for the simplest MacBook Air desk setup, with CalDigit TS4 as the strongest premium all-rounder. Choose CalDigit TS5 or TS5 Plus for future-facing Thunderbolt 5, professional networking, or storage needs; choose a compact CalDigit hub for travel; and choose Plugable UD-6950PDH only when DisplayLink’s software trade-offs are worthwhile for additional displays.

 It has two HDMI and two DisplayPort outputs, so two monitors plug straight in with ordinary cables, and one Thunderbolt 4 cable to the laptop carries both screens, 16 ports and up to 100W of charging (98W certified). On a Mac with an M4, M5 or any Pro or Max chip it extends your desktop across two 4K 60Hz screens, and a base M3 can do the same with the lid closed.  Charging is the most each dock can send to the laptop. Check it against the wattage printed on your laptop's own charger: if the dock supplies less, the laptop usually still charges, just more slowly.
 Two screens on a Mac: which docks extend and which mirror
 This is the point most dual monitor dock listings skip. A Mac can show two different screens through a dock only if two things are true.
 First, the Mac itself must support two external displays. A dock cannot raise that limit; Apple states that a hub or daisy-chaining does not increase the number of displays a Mac supports. Apple lists two external displays for MacBook Air with M4 or M5 and for MacBook Pro with M4, M4 Pro or M5, three for M5 Pro and four for M5 Max. Base M1 and M2 Macs support one, and a base M3 MacBook Air supports two only with its lid closed.
 Second, the dock must send each screen its own signal in a way macOS understands. Thunderbolt docks such as the TBT4-UDZ and TS4 do. Most plain USB-C docks with two or three video outputs, including the HP G5 and the Lenovo travel dock, split one USB-C video signal between the screens with a technique called DisplayPort Multi-Stream Transport (MST). Windows supports MST fully. macOS does not support it for extended displays, so on a Mac the screens show the same picture.
 The exception is DisplayLink. A DisplayLink dock like the Plugable UD-3900 has its own graphics chip and receives the picture as USB data through a driver, so its screens sit outside the Mac's native display count. That is why it can add two separate screens to a base M1 or M2 MacBook Air. The cost is lower resolution, no copy-protected video and some extra processor load.
 In short, for two separate screens on a Mac: buy the Plugable TBT4-UDZ or the CalDigit TS4 if your Mac has an M4, M5, Pro or Max chip, and the Plugable UD-3900 if it has a base M1 or M2. Don't buy the HP G5 or the Lenovo travel dock for a Mac. Our Thunderbolt docks guide goes further into Mac models and ports.
 Thunderbolt, USB-C or DisplayLink
 The connection type matters more than the brand.
 Thunderbolt docks (Plugable TBT4-UDZ, CalDigit TS4) carry two high-resolution screens, fast data and up to about 100W of charging on one cable, on both Macs and Windows. They need a Thunderbolt or USB4 port for their full ability. Plugged into a plain USB-C laptop they still work, but CalDigit lists one external display for the TS4 on a USB-C Windows laptop, and Plugable lists two for the TBT4-UDZ. Our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs USB4 comparison explains the port names.
 USB-C docks (HP G5, Lenovo travel dock) work with any laptop whose USB-C port supports video (DisplayPort Alt Mode) and charging. They are a good choice for Windows. On a Mac they give one screen, or several mirrored screens.
 DisplayLink docks (Plugable UD-3900) work over almost any USB 3.0 or USB-C port, need a driver, and suit spreadsheets, documents and email rather than video or games.
 Most Windows laptop owners should check one thing first: whether the laptop's USB-C port is marked Thunderbolt or USB4. If it is, buy the TBT4-UDZ. If it is plain USB-C with video, the HP G5 is the better match.
 Match the dock to your monitors
 Count the inputs on your monitors before you buy. The TBT4-UDZ takes HDMI and DisplayPort monitors directly, but not USB-C ones. The TS4 has one DisplayPort output and sends a second screen through a Thunderbolt port, which suits USB-C monitors and DisplayPort monitors with a USB-C-to-DisplayPort cable. The HP G5 and Lenovo travel dock each have DisplayPort and HDMI. The UD-3900 has two HDMI outputs and does not support DisplayPort monitors.
 Resolution limits differ too. The TBT4-UDZ and the Lenovo dock run each screen at up to 4K 60Hz. The TS4 reaches 4K 60Hz on two screens with most laptops, and up to 6K 60Hz with an M1 Pro, M1 Max or M1 Ultra Mac. The UD-3900 is limited to 1920 x 1200 on two screens. For setting the screens up once they are connected, see our dual monitor setup guide , and if you still need the monitors themselves, our best monitors for a home office guide covers sizes and connections.
 How we chose
 These recommendations are research-based. We have not tested these docks. We read each maker's own product page, product sheet or user guide for the laptop connection, number of screens, Mac support, charging and ports, and every figure here comes from those documents, linked under Sources. We looked for docks that run two monitors from one cable and that cover the common cases: a recent Mac, a Windows laptop with or without Thunderbolt, travel, and laptops that cannot drive two screens natively. An earlier version of this guide included the Kensington SD5780T and the Dell WD22TB4. Kensington now lists the SD5780T as discontinued, and Dell's US store no longer lists the WD22TB4, so we replaced both.
 We link to stores we could confirm sell each exact model; we don't compare their prices.
 Questions people ask
 Can a USB-C docking station run two monitors on a MacBook?
 Only some can. Thunderbolt docks give two separate screens on Macs that support two displays, but many plain USB-C dual monitor docks, including the HP G5 and Lenovo travel dock, use DisplayPort MST, which macOS does not support for extended displays, so both screens show the same picture.
 How do I get two monitors on a base M1 or M2 MacBook Air?
 Use a DisplayLink dock such as the Plugable UD-3900. Base M1 and M2 Macs drive only one external display natively, and a Thunderbolt dock cannot raise that, but DisplayLink sends the picture over USB as data and adds two screens at up to 1920 x 1200.
 Do I need a Thunderbolt port for a dual monitor dock?
 No. The HP G5 and Lenovo travel dock run two or more screens from a USB-C port that supports video, and the Plugable UD-3900 works over USB 3.0. A Thunderbolt or USB4 port gets the most from the Plugable TBT4-UDZ and CalDigit TS4, and on a Mac it is what gives two extended screens.
 Can a docking station charge my laptop?
 Most of these can. The TBT4-UDZ supplies up to 100W (98W certified), the TS4 up to 98W, the HP G5 up to 100W and the Lenovo travel dock up to 100W with a separate 135W USB-C adapter. The Plugable UD-3900 does not charge the laptop.
 Will a dual monitor dock play Netflix on both screens?
 The Thunderbolt and USB-C docks here use the laptop’s own video output, so streaming works as it would on a directly connected monitor. DisplayLink docks such as the Plugable UD-3900 do not support copy-protected video such as Netflix.

A Thunderbolt dock with two native video paths, whose maker lists base M4 dual-display support, works within Apple's limits. A USB-C MST dock mirrors the second screen on macOS.  What Apple documents for the M4 Air
 Up to two external displays at the same time, in addition to the built-in display.
 Two displays: up to 6K at 60Hz or 4K at 144Hz each. One display: up to 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz or 4K at 240Hz.
 Closing the lid does not add a third external display.
 A supported hub or daisy chain can carry two displays over one Thunderbolt port, but it does not raise the maximum.
 For how this differs from M1, M2, M3 and M5 models, see MacBook Air dual monitors by chip .
 Dock types compared for two extended screens
 Dock type Two extended screens on an M4 Air? What to check 
 Thunderbolt 4/5 dock with two video-capable outputs Yes, within Apple's limits The maker's Mac table lists base M4 (not only Pro/Max) for dual displays 
 USB-C MST dock ("dual HDMI" from one USB-C) No: the second screen mirrors macOS does not support MST for independent extended displays

 If you already bought a dock and both screens show the same image, read why a MacBook mirrors two monitors through a dock .
 A documented example: CalDigit TS4
 CalDigit lists base M4 and M5 Macs among the hosts that can run dual displays from the TS4, and its knowledge base says M4 and M5 MacBook Air models support dual extended monitors through a CalDigit Thunderbolt dock. The documented wiring options are:
 One monitor on the TS4's DisplayPort output and one on a spare downstream Thunderbolt 4 port (with a USB-C video adapter if needed).
 Two USB-C or Thunderbolt monitors on the two downstream Thunderbolt 4 ports.
 The TS4's other USB-C and USB-A ports are data-only, so a monitor plugged into them will not light up. CalDigit's FAQ also lists up to 4K 60Hz per screen for dual monitors on hosts other than M1 Pro/Max/Ultra, which is lower than Apple's 6K ceiling for the Mac itself. Check the dock maker's current table if you want two 5K or 6K screens. Our M4 Air dual-monitor setup walks through one exact TS4 route, and the CalDigit TS4 profile lists its conditions.
 Checklist before you buy a dock
 Confirm the chip in Apple menu > About This Mac. "M4" must be the Air's chip, not a later or earlier one.
 Ask whether you need a dock at all: two monitors on the Air's two Thunderbolt ports is the simplest documented route.
 On the dock's spec page, find a Mac table that names base M4 for two displays. "Mac: mirror only" or MST wording means one extended screen at most.
 Note the dock's dual-display resolution and refresh limit, and whether HDMI adapters cap the mode.
 After connecting, open System Settings > Displays and make sure neither screen is set to mirror.
